Learning Objectives
Describe risk factors for acute and recurrent patellar dislocation in pediatric and adolescent
patients.
Describe dynamic and static anatomic contributors to patellofemoral stability.
Describe the physical examination for patellofemoral instability.
Describe the unique anatomy of the skeletally immature knee and how it influences
management of patellofemoral instability.
Describe indications for surgical management of patellofemoral instability in pediatric and
adolescent patients.

Lateral instability most common
Common injuries occurring during a patellofemoral instability event
Torn medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) and/or medial retinaculum
Osteochondral injuries can occur as the patella relocates.

Overview
More than 90% of patellofemoral dislocation/subluxation episodes occur in a lateral
direction. Common injuries after patellofemoral instability include a torn MPFL and/or a
torn medial retinaculum. These tears are primarily femur based or patella based or
occur in the midsubstance.1 Osteochondral injuries/fractures also may occur as the
patella relocates from a laterally dislocated position. These injuries typically occur on the
lateral femoral condyle or the medial patellar facet2 and may vary in size, depth, and
specific location (eg, articulating or nonarticulating zone). Osteochondral injuries may
result in loose bodies. Bone bruising also may occur at these locations in the absence of
a displaced osteochondral fracture or loose body.
Epidemiology
The risk of sustaining a patellofemoral instability episode is highest in 10- to 19-year-olds.3
More than 50% of instability events occur during sports activity.
The risk of sustaining a recurrent instability episode after a first-time dislocation ranges from
36% to 71%.4
Recurrent instability increases the risk for patellofemoral arthritis.5
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The patella is a sesamoid bone within the knee extensor mechanism.
Usually develops two equally sized medial and lateral facets
Must be guided into the trochlea as the knee moves from extension into flexion
Patella engages the trochlea at 20° to 30° of knee flexion

2/20

The trochlea provides a bony constraint to lateral translation.
A shallow/dysplastic trochlea provides less bony restraint.
Joints, Ligaments, and Musculature
The MPFL is the primary static soft-tissue restraint to lateral patellar translation.
The medial quadriceps (vastus medialis obliquus) is the primary dynamic stabilizer to lateral
patellar translation.
A tight lateral retinaculum may predispose individuals to lateral instability.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The patella is a sesamoid bone that lies within the extensor mechanism of the knee and
usually develops two equally sized medial and lateral facets. The patella articulates with
the femoral trochlea and must be guided into the trochlea as the knee moves from
extension into flexion. The patella normally begins to engage the trochlea at
approximately 20° to 30° of knee flexion. Once the patella is engaged, the trochlea
provides a bony restraint to patellar instability; if the patella is not engaged, soft-tissue
structures provide restraint. These soft-tissue restraints include the MPFL and the
medial quadriceps (vastus medialis obliquus). Abnormal soft-tissue structures may
increase the risk of patellofemoral instability. In addition, tight structures, such as the
lateral retinaculum, may cause lateral instability, contributing to patellar instability. The
soft-tissue structures guide the patella into the trochlea as the knee moves into flexion.
A shallow or dysplastic trochlea predisposes individuals to patellofemoral instability,
even if the patella is engaged within the trochlea.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Patellofemoral subluxation or dislocation occurs from a noncontact, rotational, or valgus
moment at the time of injury or from a direct blow.
Risk Factors

An increased relative quadriceps angle (Q-angle) (Figure 1) predisposes individuals to lateral
dislocation/subluxation.6,7
Factors that increase the Q-angle
Static or dynamic genu valgum (eg, poor landing/squatting mechanics) (Figure 2)
Excess femoral anteversion
Excess external tibial torsion
Lateralized tibial tubercle (eg, increased tibial tubercle‒trochlear groove distance)
Pes planovalgus
Trochlear dysplasia
Patella alta
Previous patellar dislocation
Age younger than 18 years at time of first dislocation
Disorders that affect ligamentous laxity (eg, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Down syndrome, or
generalized ligamentous laxity)

The Q-angle is formed by a line drawn longitudinal to the quadriceps muscle and a line drawn
longitudinal to the patellar tendon. (Courtesy of Aristides Ignacio Cruz Jr, MD, MBA, FAAOS,


Risk Factors
Multiple risk factors may lead to patellofemoral instability. Anatomic factors that
increase the Q-angle may expand the lateral force vector of the extensor mechanism,
causing lateral patellofemoral dislocation. These anatomic factors include static or
dynamic genu valgum, excess femoral anteversion, excess external tibial torsion,
lateralization of the tibial tubercle, and pes planovalgus (ie, flatfeet). The trochlea also
plays an important role in patellofemoral instability. Factors that decrease the bony
restraint of the trochlea, such as dysplasia and patella alta, may undermine stability.
Finally, a history of dislocation, younger age at initial dislocation, and disorders that
affect ligamentous laxity also are risk factors for dislocation.
Associated Injuries
MPFL rupture

Medial retinaculum tear
Osteochondral fracture
Injury Classification
Traumatic patellofemoral instability is classified descriptively.
Dislocation or subluxation
Lateral or medial (lateral most common)
First time or recurrent/chronic
Obligatory patellofemoral dislocation often is associated with multiple anatomic abnormalities
or syndromes.

Injury Classification
Patellofemoral instability is described as a frank dislocation or—if the patella does not
frankly dislocate out of the patellofemoral joint—as a subluxation. The direction of
instability typically is lateral. The mechanism of injury varies. Patellofemoral instability
may result from a direct blow; however, it most often occurs from a noncontact
mechanism of injury during athletic activity. Instability also is classified as a first time or
recurrent injury, with management depending on the duration of symptoms. Obligatory
patellofemoral dislocation most often is associated with multiple anatomic abnormalities
or congenital syndromes.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
May involve a noncontact twisting mechanism or a direct blow to the knee.
With frank dislocation, the patella may spontaneously reduce, or reduction may require
positioning with the leg in hip flexion and knee extension.
Physical Examination

Point tenderness is maximal at the retinacular or ligament tear along its course from the
medial epicondyle to the medial patella.
If present, knee effusion varies in size
A large knee effusion should raise suspicion for a displaced osteochondral fracture.
Apprehension test
Lateral translation of the patella produces an impending feeling of instability.
Evaluation of axial and rotational alignment
With the patient in the prone position, femoral version and tibial torsion are assessed.
Evaluation of the Q-angle
The J sign may be appreciated (Video 1).
The patella is laterally subluxated with the knee fully extended and engages the trochlea as
the knee is flexed.
From the examiner’s perspective, the track of the patella makes an inverted J.
Video 1 Cruz AI Jr: Video: The J Sign. Providence, RI, 2020.
Differential Diagnosis
Other knee internal derangements
Anterior cruciate ligament/posterior cruciate ligament tear

Meniscal tear
Collateral ligament injury
Isolated osteochondral fracture
Unstable osteochondritis dissecans lesion
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Plain radiographs may appear normal or may demonstrate an osteochondral loose body.
Evaluate trochlear morphology and patellar height and tilt on lateral and sunrise views.
Measures of patellar height include the Insall-Salvati index, the Caton-Deschamps index, and
the Blackburne-Peel ratio (Figure 3; Resource 1).
Standing, full-length, bilateral lower extremity (hips to ankles) radiographs to assess coronal
plane alignment (Figure 4)
Figure 3 Illustrations of the knee show methods of assessing patellar height in skeletally
immature patients. A, The Caton-Deschamps index is calculated by dividing the distance between
the inferior aspect of the patellar articular facet and the anterior corner of the superior aspect of

Use of MRI after acute dislocation is controversial.
Used to evaluate for displaced osteochondral injury/loose body (Figure 5)
MRI is indicated for preoperative planning in patients with chronic patellofemoral instability.
Estimate skeletal maturity/growth remaining
Measure tibial tubercle‒trochlear groove distance
Measure trochlear morphology
Measure patellar tilt

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Initial management includes immobilization for comfort, rest, ice, compression, and elevation.
Physical therapy is initiated to strengthen the injured extremity and address core and hip
weakness, dynamic knee stabilizer (eg, vastus medialis obliquus) strengthening, and
maladaptive movement patterns (eg, dynamic genu valgum).
A patellar stabilizing brace also can be used for activities of daily living during recovery from
acute injury and for sports activity when the athlete is ready to return to play.
Evidence supporting specific types of bracing and/or immobilization is weak.8
Return to activity should be based on pain, range of motion, strength, functional milestones,
and psychological readiness.

Nonsurgical Management
The standard of care for first-time lateral patellar instability remains nonsurgical
management. Patients should be counseled that the risk of recurrent dislocation
remains relatively high, particularly if other anatomic abnormalities, such as patella alta,
trochlear dysplasia, or genu valgum, are present.
Surgical Management
Indications
Osteochondral injury with loose body
Recurrent/chronic instability
Failure of nonsurgical management with persistent, functionally limiting pain or instability
Contraindications
Open physes require growth-respecting modification of patellofemoral stabilization
techniques

Procedures that will compromise an open physis, such as tibial tubercle osteotomy,
transphyseal distal femoral drilling for MPFL reconstruction, and tracheoplasty, are
contraindicated.
Techniques/Procedures
Procedures depend on the constellation of symptoms and radiographic abnormalities (Video
2).
À la carte procedures to manage specific anatomic abnormalities
Lateral release
Medial retinacular or MPFL repair
Medial plication or advancement of vastus medialis obliquus fascia
MPFL reconstruction (Figure 6)
Medial quadriceps tendon–femoral ligament reconstruction9
Guided growth with hemiepiphysiodesis to manage genu valgum in skeletally immature
patients
Distal femoral osteotomy to manage genu valgum in skeletally mature patients
Derotational osteotomy of the femur and/or tibia
Loose body removal or open reduction and internal fixation of an osteochondral fragment
Tibial tubercle osteotomy in skeletally mature patients for increased tibial tubercle trochlear
groove distance
Patellar ligament medialization without osteotomy (eg, Roux-Goldthwait procedure) in
skeletally immature patients
Special considerations in skeletally immature patients10
MPFL femoral insertion
Shea et al11 investigated the origin of the MPFL in skeletally immature knees.
The center of the MPFL origin was distal to the distal femoral physis in most skeletally
immature specimens (23 of 36 specimens).
In older specimens, the proximal extent was above the physis.
Sochacki et al12 examined the relationship between the MPFL origin and the distal femoral
physis.
The MPFL originated distal to the distal femoral physis in 92.8% of skeletally immature
knees.
The mean distance from the physis was 6.9 mm (± 2.4 mm).

Complications
Arthrofibrosis
Recurrent lateral patellofemoral dislocation
Distal femoral growth disturbance13
Overcorrection of axial or rotational malalignment
Iatrogenic medial patellofemoral dislocation
Postoperative Rehabilitation
Immediate–weight bearing locked in extension is allowed.
Range of motion should be restricted to 0° to 90° for 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively.
Early physical therapy is important for quadriceps activation and range of motion.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:33 PM
AAOS | Patellofemoral Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000033
15/20

Return to sports or activities may occur after strength and neuromuscular control have
returned. In general, this will occur approximately 6 months postoperatively.
A patellar-stabilizing brace may be used for return to play.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Osteochondral injuries should be addressed.
Management depends on the size and location of the injury.
Osteochondral loose body smaller than 1 cm = excision
Osteochondral loose body larger than 1 cm = consider reduction and fixation
Fixation options
Metal screws, bioabsorbable screws/implants
Salvage options
Osteochondral autograft, osteochondral allograft, cartilage repair procedures (eg,
autologous chondrocyte implantation)
Anatomic abnormalities that are risk factors for dislocation should be evaluated and
addressed if possible.
For optimal outcomes, anatomic reconstruction of the MPFL is important.
Tension of the construct is set with the patella centered in the trochlea and with the knee in
30° to 40° of flexion.
Graft attachment sites on the patella and femur should assessed to ensure they produce an
isometric graft with the knee in 0° to 60° of flexion.
The femoral attachment can be within 1 to 3 mm from the epiphyseal plate. Femoral drill
tunnels should be aimed away from the physis. The drill will be aimed distal and posterior if
starting below the physis (Figure 7).
Avoid overconstraining the patella. The patella should have one or two quadrants of medial
and lateral translation after repair, similar to the native patella. With overtensioning of the
repair or reconstruction, flexion past 90° will be difficult.
Excessive lateral release may result in iatrogenic medial instability or dislocation.
Tibial tubercle osteotomy should be avoided in skeletally immature patients to prevent tibial
tubercle growth disturbance and resultant recurvatum deformity.
